items.label: text
items.text: You may sometimes see these plotted as smooth graphs, but that is technically wrong. A smooth curve should only be used for a continuous independent variable, one which can take any value. There is no such thing as an alcohol with 0.5 or 1.64 carbon atoms! The number of carbon atoms is a non-continuous variable because it can only take whole number values.

items.label: text
items.text: That doesn't mean you can't use this experiment to make useful comparisons. If yourepeat it with other alcohols, under conditions that are as similar as possible, you can find how the heat evolved (given out) changes as the alcohol gets bigger.

items.label: text
items.text: In Figure 19.11 we can see that the combustion reaction gets more exothermic as the alcohol chain becomes longer. In other words, longer alcohols give out more heat energy per mole when they burn than shorter ones.

items.label: text
items.text: The increase in the heat evolved as alcohol chain lengthens is regular. The difference between one alcohol and the next is always an extra CH2 (see Chapter26, page 288, for more detail on the structures of alcohols), and so the number of extra bonds broken and made (see below) increases in a regular way. That means that the heat evolved will also increase in a regular way.

items.label: section_header
items.text: WORKING OUT ENTHALPY CHANGES FOR REACTIONS INVOLVING SOLUTIONS USING CALORIMETRY EXPERIMENTS

items.label: text
items.text: You can use very similar methods for measuring molar enthalpy changes in displacement reactions (e.g. zinc and copper(ll) sulfate solution), dissolving (e.g. dissolving ammonium chloride in water to form a solution) and neutralisation reactions (e.g. between potassium hydroxide solution and dilute hydrochloric acid). These experiments also involve heating water, but this time the water is part of the solutions we are using. We will look at how to do this in the next few practicals.
